description:
FlareForge is a passionate team of young innovators from Ghana competing in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our project, FireScope AI, aims to transform NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite data into meaningful insights about wildfire activity. Through data science, AI, and interactive visualizations, we seek to identify fire patterns, support environmental monitoring, and help protect communities across Africa and beyond.

FlareForge: Born in Ghana. Built for Earth. Powered by Space.
summary:
FireScope AI is a web research workspace that helps students and researchers explore NASA MODIS and VIIRS
fire observations in Ghana. It combines an interactive map, an activity calendar, original source records and
evidence exports. To address cross-sensor consistency, a transparent experiment compares 75,823
observations from 50 sampled days across 2021-2025, using separate training, validation and test years. A
separate 2024-2025 archive contains 549,208 observations across 731 requested dates and compares monthly
detection counts with NASA mapped burned area where source data are complete. Missing coverage and
quality limitations remain visible. FireScope makes satellite records easier to inspect and compare without
treating detections as individual fires or claiming validated fire-risk prediction.
details: The problem MODIS and VIIRS measure thermal activity at different resolutions, sensitivities and acquisition times. Changes in raw detection counts can reflect instrument differences as well as changes in burning. Researchers need a way to trace calendar patterns back to source observations and understand what is missing. What the project does FireScope AI provides an interactive map, area/date/sensor filters, an activity calendar, original-record inspection, local CSV import and CSV/PDF/evidence exports. NASA true-color imagery supplies date-linked visual context. A separate archive covers requested dates in 2024-2025 for three rectangular study extents: Ghana, Northern Ghana and Tamale. These are study rectangles, not administrative boundaries. How the sensor experiment works The frozen experiment uses 75,823 NASA standard-processing records from the first five January and July days of each year in 2021-2025. Daily occupied 0.1-degree cells are compared between VIIRS Suomi-NPP and MODIS Aqua. A nonnegative scale through the origin is fitted on 2021-2023, validated on 2024 and tested on 2025. Training-only seasonal means provide a simpler baseline; original data and checksum provenance remain inspectable. What the results show Across ten held-out 2025 days, mean absolute disagreement with Aqua is 266.1 occupied cells/day for raw VIIRS, 76.9 for the seasonal baseline and 70.9 for adjusted VIIRS. This shows closer agreement with a reference sensor on that sample. It is not independent validation of fire-detection accuracy. Historical and burned-area comparison The separate archive contains 549,208 deduplicated observations across 731 requested dates. Monthly NASA MCD64A1.061 rasters supply mapped burned area and quality measures. Area totals are available for 18 months; six months with incomplete source tiles remain unavailable rather than becoming zero. Native raster pixel areas and QA flags are used. Benefits and intended outcomes Students and researchers can inspect both sensors, distinguish unknown coverage from returned zero detections, explore historical patterns and export traceable evidence. We aim to improve research interpretation and reproducibility. Next steps include observing-opportunity metadata, independent reference events, uncertainty assessment and geographic-transfer evaluation. User benefit and field performance have not been independently measured. Tools and limits React, TypeScript, Vite, Leaflet, Node.js, Papa Parse and GeoTIFF.js support the workflow; Firebase Hosting serves the public demo. The public release uses saved data and local imports; private live fire, weather, news and place-search services are disconnected there. A detection is not a distinct fire. Request completion does not prove cloud-free observing opportunity, and MCD64A1 is not an independent active-fire reference. No validated forecast or emergency alert is provided.
